title: Eliminate decommissioning: memory sleds outlive three CPU generations
idea: Eliminate the assumption that DRAM retires with its server: hyperscalers move bulk DDR into CXL-attached memory sleds on a 10-year depreciation schedule and swap only CPU/accelerator sleds every 3-4 years, inserting a retimer/protocol-bridge card at each refresh.
why: Fleet refresh scraps DIMMs at year 4-5 although bits last >10 years; decoupling cuts new-DRAM demand per refresh cycle ~30-50% with zero new wafers.

title: Eliminate the package: decap scrap modules, rebond known-good DRAM die
idea: Eliminate the package as a one-way trip: laser plus fuming-acid decapsulation strips mold compound from scrapped DRAM packages, freed dies are re-probed on wafer-sort-style chucks, re-bumped, and re-assembled into new multi-die packages or chiplet substrates.
why: Recovers bits whose EUV/capex cost is already sunk (die is ~85% of module cost); even partial recovery of e-waste DRAM adds a few percent of annual bit supply at low capital.

title: Eliminate the scrap bin: JEDEC bank-disable map for partial-good dies
idea: Eliminate binary pass/fail dies: a JEDEC-standard on-die fuse map records disabled banks/subarrays, and memory controllers plus the OS allocate around them, so a die with one dead bank ships as a 7/8-capacity part instead of being crushed or sold grey.
why: Unrepairable clustered defects cost ~2-6% of wafer bits; harvesting them is like adding a mid-size fab's output at zero capex.

title: Eliminate the silicon wafer: memory tiles on idle display-glass lines
idea: Eliminate the 300mm wafer and the DRAM fab: retool overbuilt Gen-6/8 LCD/OLED backplane lines (oxide-TFT tools already installed) to build 8-16 stacked tiers of low-temperature oxide-TFT gain-cell arrays on glass, diced into cheap capacity tiles for CXL far memory.
why: Panel area costs ~100x less per cm2 than 300mm silicon and lines are depreciated; with tier stacking, capacity-tier cost per bit could approach DRAM with almost no new capex and no EUV.

title: Eliminate the IDM: fabless DRAM tolled on mature logic foundries
idea: Eliminate the integrated DRAM manufacturer: a fabless house designs logic-compatible high-retention DRAM (MIM-capacitor 1T1C or capacitorless) for 22-40nm logic processes and buys wafers from under-utilized foundries, the way fabless modem makers did.
why: Taps the ~20-30% idle mature-node foundry capacity, including US sites, for embedded/industrial DRAM without a $15B fab.

title: Eliminate leading-edge wafers for legacy demand: restart mothballed DUV lines
idea: Eliminate serving DDR3/DDR4/LPDDR4 demand from leading-edge fabs: acquire mothballed or exiting 300mm lines and run 2x-nm DUV-only DRAM (zero EUV) for auto, industrial and networking, so leading fabs stop diverting wafers to legacy parts.
why: Legacy parts are rising fastest in price; a depreciated DUV line costs ~10-20% of greenfield per wafer start and avoids the single-supplier EUV chokepoint.

title: Eliminate the cleanroom building: sealed-pod minimal fabs in warehouses
idea: Eliminate the ballroom cleanroom: adopt the minimal-fab model (half-inch wafers in sealed shuttles, shoebox tools with local mini-environments) to make radiation-hard, automotive and defense DRAM in ordinary industrial buildings.
why: Line capex falls from billions to ~$10-50M for low-volume, high-value memory; slashes water and HVAC energy; onshores defense memory.

title: Eliminate helium from the DRAM fab bill of materials
idea: Eliminate helium: replace He backside cooling in etch/CVD electrostatic chucks with H2 or H2/Ar mixes (H2 conducts heat ~1.2x better than He) with chuck seal redesign, and membrane-recapture any residual He at tool exhaust.
why: Qatar's ~30% of helium supply is offline since March 2026; removing He from the critical path protects wafer starts.

title: Eliminate the quartz crucible: cold-crucible levitation silicon growth
idea: Eliminate the Spruce Pine high-purity-quartz crucible: grow large-diameter ingots in water-cooled segmented copper cold crucibles where induction fields push the melt off the wall so silicon touches only its own frozen skull.
why: Removes a >80% single-site chokepoint; lower oxygen content also reduces thermal donors that hurt DRAM retention.

title: Eliminate one-ingot-per-wafer: reusable donor wafers via porous-silicon transfer
idea: Eliminate consuming a full prime wafer per lot: grow device-grade epitaxial silicon on a porous-silicon release layer over a donor, bond it to lower-grade handle wafers, cleave, and reuse each donor 10-20 times.
why: Cuts prime polysilicon, crucible and ingot demand ~5-10x per wafer start; DRAM arrays need only the top tens of microns of perfect silicon.

title: Eliminate virgin tungsten: fab-scrap metals loop plus molybdenum swap
idea: Eliminate the mine-to-fab dependency: a US recovery loop refines spent W/Ta/Ru sputter targets (typically only ~30-40% consumed), chamber shields and CVD-W residue back to 6N purity, paired with qualified Mo wordline/contact substitution.
why: China holds ~80% of tungsten; ~60-70% of each target is recoverable, sharply reducing import exposure.

title: Eliminate phantom orders: privacy-preserving demand ledger kills the bullwhip
idea: Eliminate double- and triple-ordering: OEMs, distributors and makers post orders into a secure-multiparty-computation ledger that de-duplicates the same end demand arriving through multiple channels, so producers see true demand without revealing customer secrets.
why: Shortage panics inflate orders ~20-40% and starve small buyers; truthful demand redirects existing supply to real users and prevents the following glut.

title: Eliminate DIMM ownership: cascade leasing priced per GB-month
idea: Eliminate end users buying DIMMs: a lessor owns modules, bills per GB-month, recovers them at each refresh, re-tests and cascades them down tiers (cloud, enterprise, edge, schools), financing the fleet with asset-backed securities.
why: Cascading keeps each bit in service 10-15 years instead of 5, cutting new-bit demand ~15-25% in mature segments.

title: Eliminate soldered-equals-scrap: robotic LPDDR harvesting from e-waste boards
idea: Eliminate shredding of phones and laptops with soldered LPDDR: vision-guided robots locally reflow, lift, clean and reball LPDDR packages, test them on socketed ATE, and sell graded parts to low-cost tablet, IoT and SBC makers.
why: LPDDR is roughly a third of DRAM bits and nearly all of it is shredded; harvesting a slice of 3-5-year-old devices yields supply at ~10-20% of new cost.

title: Eliminate factory final test: in-field BIST screening and soft repair
idea: Eliminate long DRAM final test and burn-in: dies ship after short wafer sort, carrying on-die BIST and soft post-package repair, and finish retention and pattern screening inside the customer's system during the first weeks of operation.
why: Test is ~10-15% of DRAM cost and ATE is a capacity bottleneck; cutting test time raises output throughput ~20-30% with existing testers.

title: Eliminate the boom-bust cycle: allied strategic DRAM reserve
idea: Eliminate the price cycle that suppresses investment: a US/allied agency buys packaged DRAM and wafers in gluts, stores them in dry nitrogen, and releases them inside a price band in shortages, like a petroleum reserve.
why: A 2-3 month reserve would blunt 4x price spikes and let makers commit capex counter-cyclically.

title: Eliminate equity-funded fabs: take-or-pay prepayments collateralize fab bonds
idea: Eliminate funding fabs from equity at the cycle top: hyperscalers sign 7-10-year take-or-pay bit contracts that, like LNG offtake agreements, collateralize project-finance bonds for a dedicated US fab SPV.
why: Lowers cost of capital ~3-5 points on a $15B fab where depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost.

title: Eliminate process secrecy: open DRAM PDK and periphery IP
idea: Eliminate closed DRAM know-how: fund an open PDK for a 1T1C stacked-capacitor process at a mature US node (40-65nm) plus open sense-amp, decoder and refresh-controller IP so startups and universities can tape out real DRAM.
why: Cuts entry cost for specialty DRAM from billions to millions and rebuilds a US DRAM talent pipeline.

title: Eliminate the patent thicket: public commons from distressed DRAM portfolios
idea: Eliminate royalty barriers: a public-private fund buys DRAM patent portfolios from exited or bankrupt players and licenses them royalty-free to any US-made memory entrant, with pooled defensive countersuit rights.
why: Removes litigation risk that deters new DRAM entrants; one portfolio buy can protect a dozen startups.

title: Eliminate single-product fabs: dual-qualified NAND/DRAM swing lines
idea: Eliminate the fixed product mix: pre-qualify shared tool sets (much of litho, etch and deposition overlaps) with both DRAM and NAND recipes and reserve slots for DRAM-only tools, allowing a 3-6-month swing to DRAM when NAND is in glut.
why: Turns existing NAND overcapacity into DRAM supply in months instead of 3-5 years.

title: Eliminate dummy monitor wafers with in-situ virtual metrology
idea: Eliminate the monitor, dummy and seasoning wafers that eat wafer starts: in-chamber optical emission and RF sensors plus virtual metrology qualify tools on product wafers, keeping reclaimed monitors only for audits.
why: Frees ~5-10% of fab wafer capacity and the matching substrate and crucible demand.

title: Eliminate photomasks: multi-beam direct write for low-volume DRAM
idea: Eliminate $10-30M mask sets for small-lot memory: multi-beam e-beam writers expose critical layers directly for specialty DRAM (rad-hard, automotive, custom HBM base dies), allowing per-wafer design changes.
why: Removes mask capital as a barrier to new entrants; throughput is low but adequate for <1k wafers/month niches.

title: Eliminate the arms-length buyer: OEM cooperative co-owns a DRAM fab
idea: Eliminate the pure-buyer role: automotive, industrial and PC OEMs form a cooperative, like farm co-ops or airline fuel consortia, that owns a mid-size legacy-node DRAM fab and allocates output at cost by equity share.
why: Guarantees allocation in shortages and spreads capex across many balance sheets.

title: Eliminate test hardware: bootable signed DIMM health certificate
idea: Eliminate expensive ATE for used-memory trust: a free bootable image runs 8-hour retention, pattern and row-hammer tests on any host and signs the result with the module's SPD serial; ~$600k builds the software, signing service and three pilot broker integrations in 18 months.
why: Trust is the bottleneck in reuse; certified used DRAM sells at 40-60% of new and unlocks stranded DDR4 inventory.

title: Eliminate RMA scrapping: bad-row map stored in module SPD
idea: Eliminate discarding DIMMs with a few failing rows: an open firmware/Linux patch learns failing rows from correctable-error telemetry and writes a compact retirement map into spare SPD EEPROM bytes, so every future host offlines those pages; ~$300k, 12 months, upstreamed to Linux and coreboot.
why: Most fleet DIMM replacements (~1-3%/year) are few-row faults; keeping them in service saves petabytes per hyperscaler.

title: Eliminate overprovisioning: working-set audit with shared-savings DIMM resale
idea: Eliminate padded memory configs: a startup deploys eBPF working-set profilers across a customer's fleet for 60 days, proves which DIMMs are never touched, pulls them, and resells them, splitting proceeds; $1M funds tooling plus five enterprise pilots.
why: Enterprise servers often touch only 40-60% of installed DRAM; freeing 20% at 4x prices pays customers and adds supply at once.

title: Eliminate wafer-reject destruction: rescue dies with tiny remap controller
idea: Eliminate crushing of ink-dotted DRAM dies: buy reject and downgrade wafers at scrap price, characterize dies on rented probers, and pair each with a small address-remap controller in a system-in-package for embedded buyers; $1M covers prober time, OSAT lots and controller design.
why: Recovers bits otherwise destroyed (a few percent of output) for buyers who value availability over density.

title: Eliminate retention-fail scrap: sell weak dies as fast-refresh grade
idea: Eliminate the 64 ms retention gate: dies that fail 64 ms but pass 16-32 ms are bought, binned and sold with an SPD flag that forces the controller's existing 2x/4x refresh mode; ~$400k for binning and qualification.
why: Converts retention-tail rejects into usable bits for bandwidth-insensitive capacity tiers at a small refresh-energy penalty.

title: Eliminate the 85C margin: cold-only DRAM grade for liquid racks
idea: Eliminate the worst-case temperature spec: dies failing at 85-95C but passing at 45C are certified Cold-Grade for direct-liquid-cooled racks with guaranteed coolant temperature and on-DIMM thermal shutdown; $1M funds binning, sensors and one data-center pilot.
why: Retention roughly doubles per ~10C cooler, so thermal-screen rejects become usable bits as liquid cooling spreads.

title: Eliminate perfect-bit requirement: Grade-C DRAM for error-tolerant workloads
idea: Eliminate the near-zero-error spec where it does not matter: modules with measured raw BER ~1e-12 to 1e-9 are sold for CDN video caches and checkpoint staging protected by software CRC and re-fetch; ~$500k pilot with one CDN.
why: Widens usable bin yield; cache workloads simply re-fetch on a CRC miss.

title: Eliminate royalty fear: expired-patent freedom-to-operate atlas for legacy DRAM
idea: Eliminate the belief that DRAM is a legal minefield: a ~$400k legal-engineering project maps expired pre-2006 DRAM patents onto a complete 50-90nm stacked-capacitor process and periphery, publishing an open freedom-to-operate atlas and reference flow.
why: Cuts legal cost for any legacy-node entrant from millions to near zero, enabling US micro-fabs and foundries.

title: Eliminate the R&D lab: $1M prize for open gain-cell macro
idea: Eliminate hiring a research team: a $750k inducement prize plus $250k shuttle credits rewards the first open-source gain-cell DRAM macro on US open PDKs reaching >=10 ms retention and <=20 ns access, judged on silicon within 24 months.
why: Prizes typically pull 5-10x the purse in outside effort and yield a free, US-fabricable embedded DRAM block.

title: Eliminate shred-everything policy: volatile-memory sanitization clause
idea: Eliminate the security rule that sends decommissioned DRAM to shredders: a ~$300k study measures room-temperature data remanence after power-off and drives a 'power-cycled DRAM is sanitized' clause with a verification test into NIST SP 800-88 guidance and corporate disposal policies.
why: Many enterprises shred all memory by default; one policy change releases millions of DIMMs a year for reuse.

title: Eliminate price opacity: public DRAM contract index and cash-settled swaps
idea: Eliminate opaque bilateral pricing: a ~$700k startup gathers anonymized contract and spot trades from buyers, publishes a daily DRAM bit index, and partners with a commodity broker to offer cash-settled swaps.
why: Hedging lets OEMs lock costs and producers fund capacity against a forward curve, damping the cycle.

title: Eliminate the 5-year refresh: DIMM life-extension insurance
idea: Eliminate refresh-driven DIMM retirement: a managing general agent prices a policy from fleet correctable-error telemetry covering failures of DIMMs kept in service in years 6-9; $1M builds the actuarial model, a carrier partnership and two pilots.
why: Keeping DRAM 2-3 years longer cuts replacement demand ~25-40% in that segment.

title: Eliminate laptop-memory dead end: SO-DIMM-to-CXL carrier card
idea: Eliminate the form-factor dead end of laptop memory: an FPGA-based CXL Type-3 card hosts eight mixed DDR4 SO-DIMMs harvested from e-waste laptops and presents them to modern servers as a slow capacity tier; $1M covers board design, controller IP and a 200-card pilot.
why: Turns e-waste SO-DIMMs into server far-memory at a fraction of new DDR5 cost.

title: Eliminate small-buyer spot premium: purchasing cooperative pools OEM demand
idea: Eliminate spot-market exposure for small OEMs: a ~$500k-funded purchasing co-op aggregates 50-200 small hardware makers' forecasts into contract-size volumes, holds a shared rolling buffer, and allocates by commitment.
why: Small buyers pay spot premiums of 30-100% in shortages; pooling wins contract pricing and allocation.

title: Eliminate repeat qualification: shared reliability dataset for substitute DRAM
idea: Eliminate 12-24-month per-OEM requalification when switching DRAM sources: a consortium runs one automotive-grade stress dataset per part (HTOL, temperature cycling, ESD) and shares it under a common audit, so members switch to available parts in weeks; $1M funds lab time for ~40 parts.
why: Makes existing alternative supply usable quickly instead of waiting for a qualified part.

title: Eliminate single-sourced footprints: universal multi-vendor DRAM board footprint
idea: Eliminate board respins when one DRAM part disappears: publish an open reference footprint and routing that accepts LPDDR4X, DDR4 x16 and LPDDR5 packages via option resistors and a small interposer, validated on three SoC platforms; ~$400k.
why: Lets designers buy whatever DRAM is in stock, widening the effective supply pool.

title: Eliminate forced DDR5 migration: new DDR4 boards for dual-support CPUs
idea: Eliminate the platform change that strands DDR4: contract an ODM to build new DDR4 boards for CPUs and embedded SoCs whose controllers support both DDR4 and DDR5, aimed at the reclaimed-DDR4 pool; ~$800k NRE and first batch.
why: Gives used DDR4 a large new home and moves buyers off scarce DDR5.

title: Eliminate software bloat: memory-footprint bounties for top open-source apps
idea: Eliminate wasted bytes: a $1M bounty fund pays per verified MB saved, times installed base, for merged patches that cut resident memory in Chromium, Electron, Firefox, Kubernetes components and JVM defaults, measured on a public benchmark.
why: A 10% cut in browser/Electron memory across billions of devices frees hundreds of PB of effective capacity and delays RAM upgrades.

title: Eliminate external DRAM from low-end devices: MCU redesign service
idea: Eliminate the DRAM chip from products that never needed Linux: a consultancy with an open template library ports low-end routers, thermostats and HMIs from 128-512MB DDR boards to MCU, on-chip SRAM and XIP flash designs; $1M seeds ten conversions.
why: Billions of IoT units carry legacy DDR; removing it frees legacy-node supply for critical uses.

title: Eliminate the cleanroom for R&D: glovebox micro-line for oxide-TFT memory
idea: Eliminate the cleanroom for prototyping: a ~$700k line of nitrogen gloveboxes with sputter, ALD and maskless laser direct-write on 100mm glass builds low-temperature oxide-TFT 2T0C arrays to prove yield per dollar within 24 months.
why: Proves capital-light memory manufacturing at ~1/1000 of fab capex before scaling.

title: Eliminate lost know-how: retired DRAM engineers' knowledge guild
idea: Eliminate relearning lost US DRAM know-how: a ~$400k program records structured process-knowledge interviews with retired engineers from closed US and European DRAM fabs, builds a searchable knowledge base, and runs a paid advisory guild for new entrants.
why: Shortens new-entrant learning curves by years; tacit yield knowledge is the scarcest asset after capital.

title: Eliminate desoldering: old smartphone boards as ARM microserver nodes
idea: Eliminate extraction of soldered LPDDR entirely: refurbish 4-8GB smartphone logic boards (battery removed, USB-PD power, Ethernet over USB-C) into rack microserver nodes running containerized CI and edge workloads; $1M pilots 5,000 nodes.
why: Reuses DRAM and SoC together, offloading workloads that would otherwise consume new server DRAM.

title: Eliminate trusted distributors: retention fingerprints authenticate genuine DRAM
idea: Eliminate the need for authorized channels: each die's retention-failure map at deliberately reduced refresh acts as a physical unclonable fingerprint, recorded at first test in a ~$500k registry, so any buyer's software can re-measure and authenticate a part.
why: Counterfeit and remarked parts scare buyers off secondary supply; cheap authentication makes that supply usable.
